pass_a_gloss: He says in the ecclesiastical preaching the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to living well and fleeing from sin in every way, so that we may understand, having been consoled by the Lord, the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what the self-moved is, it is necessary to unfold the concept of it, so that with this having been clarified, what is being sought may be precisely presented. For of the things being moved, some have in themselves the cause of the movement, and others are moved only from outside. Then the things being carried are moved only from outside, such as wood and stones and all matter held together by habit only. But let the movement of bodies be left out of the discussion for now, since there is no need of this for the present subject. And animals and plants and all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved in themselves: from which they say metals are, and besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of being moved in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, and others from outside themselves: from outside themselves the non-living things, and from themselves the living things. And the living things are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring and provoking an impulse. And again in some of the animals, fantasies occur provoking an impulse, the imaginative nature moving the impulse in an orderly way, as in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the imaginative nature of the spider moving it in an orderly way to this very thing, and no other thing is believed by the animal besides its imaginative nature, and in the bee to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason in relation to its imaginative nature, approving and rejecting fantasies, so that the animal may be led according to them. Whence, since in the nature of reason there are starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following which, having contemplated the good and the bad, we choose the good and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, and blameworthy according to the opposite. It should not be unknown, however, that the majority of the nature ordered to all things is in the animals, and for the most part or for the lesser part, so that it is near, so to speak, to the work of the rational in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing that occurs to us from outside, moving a fantasy in us, is not among the things in our power. But to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise, is the work of our reason, either working in us according to the starting points towards the impulses provoked to the good and duty, or turning us away to the opposite.

choices.term: ὁ περὶ χρίσεως δικαίας ϑεοῦ λόγος

pass_b_english: The author notes that the church's preaching contains a message about God's righteous anointing, and that this message — believed to be true — also provokes people to live well and to flee from sin in every way, so that we may grasp, with the Lord's comfort, the most necessary problem.
In order to understand what 'self-moved' means, it is necessary to unfold the concept, so that once it is clarified, what is being sought can be precisely presented.
Among things that are moved, some have the cause of their movement within themselves, while others are moved only from outside.
Things that are carried — such as wood, stones, and all matter held together merely by habit — are moved only from outside.
The question of bodily movement is set aside for now, since it is not needed for the present subject.

Animals, plants, and in general all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved within themselves; from this class they say metals come, and besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well.

Among things that have the cause of being moved within themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from themselves in a different sense: the non-living are moved from themselves, the living from themselves.
Living things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs and provokes an impulse.

Again, in some animals fantasies arise that provoke impulses, with the imaginative nature moving the impulse in an orderly way — as in the spider, where a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the spider's imaginative nature moving it in an orderly way to that very thing, and the animal believing nothing else beyond its imaginative nature; likewise in the bee, toward shaping wax.
But the rational animal also has reason alongside its imaginative nature, a reason that judges fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them.

Since the nature of reason contains starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following them we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad; thus we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to practicing the good, and blameworthy when we do the opposite.

It should not be overlooked, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered toward all things exists in animals, whether to a greater or lesser degree, so that it comes near, so to speak, to the rational work found in tracking dogs and war horses.
For what befalls us from outside, moving a fantasy in us one way or another, is admittedly not among the things in our power.

But to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us — either operating according to the starting points that drive us toward impulses provoked to the good and to duty, or turning us away toward the opposite.

review.notes: Pass B fails on agency and accuracy regarding the distinction between 'from themselves' and 'from outside themselves' in the description of living/non-living things. The Greek states: 'τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν ἐξ ξαυτῶν μὲν τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' (the non-living from outside themselves, the living from themselves). Pass B translates this as: 'the non-living are moved from themselves, the living from themselves', which is a contradiction of the source and removes the distinction between 'ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν' (from outside themselves) and 'ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν' (from themselves).
reasons: Pass B misrepresents the Greek distinction between the movement of non-living and living things: 'τὰ δὲ ἀφ᾽ ξαυτῶν ἐξ ξαυτῶν μὲν τὰ ἄψυχα, ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῶν δὲ τὰ ἔμψυχα' (the non-living from outside themselves, the living from themselves) is rendered as 'the non-living are moved from themselves, the living from themselves', which is a logical error and a failure of accuracy.
